Reshape recurrent-event data into gap-time episodes for the backward joint model

Source: R/buildRecurrentEpisodes.R
buildRecurrentEpisodes.Rd

Experimental. Prepares recurrent-event data for the backward joint model by a gap-time (renewal) reformulation: it splits each subject's event history into episodes – the interval from one restart (the previous event, or the discharge from the stay it began) to the next event, with the clock reset to 0 at the start of each – and re-clocks any accompanying longitudinal measurements onto the same per-episode timeline. The result plugs into the existing survivalSub()/ longitudinalSub()/predictRisk() pipeline, unchanged, to predict for a subject currently at risk in an open episode whether their next event (within a horizon) is a recurrence or a terminal event; predictRecurrentCount builds on the same data to predict the number of recurrences in a window. Unlike the single-event and competing-risks methods the rest of the package rests on (Shen and Li, 2021; Li et al., 2026 – see citation("BJM")), this extension is unpublished, and has been checked only in simulation studies, not on real data (see the "Recurrent events" article on the package website).

Usage

buildRecurrentEpisodes(
  data_events,
  data_long = NULL,
  id_variable = "id",
  time_variable = "time",
  status_variable = "status",
  time_variable_long = NULL,
  episode_variable = "episode",
  gap_variable = "gap",
  time_in_episode_variable = "time_in_episode",
  event_any_variable = "event_any",
  event_type_variable = "event_type",
  restart_variable = NULL,
  lookback = 0,
  episode_id_variable = "episode_id"
)

Arguments

data_events

One row per subject per event-or-censoring occurrence, in calendar time (i.e. not yet re-clocked to gap time – this function does that). Must contain id_variable, time_variable (numeric, strictly increasing within each subject), and status_variable (0 = censored/end of follow-up, 1 = recurrent event, 2 = terminal event – the same 0/1/2 convention pbc3's status5 already uses). Any other columns are covariates, carried through to episode_data from the row that ends each episode: so a covariate that changes over time must hold, on each row, its value at the start of the episode that row ends (see Details), not its value at the event. Subjects are matched across data_events and data_long by the printed value of their id, so an id that is a number in one table and a factor or character in the other still matches; id keeps the type it has in data_events.

data_long

Optional repeated-measurement data to re-clock onto the same per-episode timeline, in the same format longitudinalSub()/ predictRisk() accept elsewhere in this package: a single bare data.frame, or a list of data.frames (one per longitudinal outcome). Must contain id_variable and time_variable_long. Rows whose time_variable_long falls outside every episode – before 0 (beyond lookback), in a hospital stay lookback does not reach, or after the subject's process has already ended (per data_events) – are dropped, with a message reporting how many. A row whose time_variable_long falls exactly on the shared boundary between two episodes (e.g. a biomarker drawn at the same visit an event is recorded) is genuinely ambiguous – it is at once "the last measurement of the ending episode" and "the first (time_in_episode = 0) measurement of the next one" – so it is kept twice, once per episode, rather than silently assigned to only one (which would systematically discard every fresh-episode baseline measurement that happens to coincide with the previous episode's event time, and bias the fitted backward-covariate effect); a message says how many rows this applies to.

id_variable, time_variable, status_variable

Column names in data_events (defaults "id", "time", "status").

time_variable_long

Column name of the measurement time in data_long; defaults to time_variable (i.e. the same name as in data_events) when NULL.

episode_variable, gap_variable, time_in_episode_variable, event_any_variable, event_type_variable, episode_id_variable

Column names to create in the output (defaults "episode", "gap", "time_in_episode", "event_any", "event_type", "episode_id"). episode_id is "<id>:<episode>" (a factor), one value per episode: the grouping variable to use for the biomarker model's random effects (see Details). Change these if they collide with an existing column of data_events/data_long – collisions are an error, not a silent overwrite.

restart_variable

Optional name of a numeric column of data_events: for each recurrence (status == 1) row, the time the process restarts after it (for hospitalizations, the discharge ending that stay; must not be earlier than the row's time_variable). The next episode starts there instead of at the event time. NULL (default) restarts at the event time itself. A missing value on a recurrence row that starts another episode is taken as no stay, with a warning; a column with no value at all is allowed. A death or the end of follow-up at or before the restart time happened during the stay: see Details. Ignored on rows that end the process. Not carried into episode_data.

lookback

A single non-negative number (Inf allowed): how far before an episode's start its measurements are still kept, as negative time_in_episode, but never from before the previous event. Default 0 keeps only measurements from the start on.

Value

A list with elements:

episode_data

One row per subject per episode: id_variable, episode_variable (episode number, starting at 1), gap_variable (that episode's gap time), event_any_variable (0/1: did the episode end in an event of either type, i.e. is gap an observed event time rather than an administrative censoring time), event_type_variable (0 = recurrence, 1 = terminal event, NA when event_any == 0), and every other column of data_events.

long_data

NULL if data_long was not supplied; otherwise data_long, in the same bare-data.frame-or-list shape it was supplied in, with episode_variable, gap_variable, time_in_episode_variable, event_any_variable, and event_type_variable columns added (and out-of-range rows dropped, as described above). Any other column of episode_data (baseline or event-time-varying covariates, e.g. age/sex) is also carried onto matching rows here, the way every row of pbc3's long-format table already repeats age/sex/years/status3 – but only into a column data_long does not already have of that name.

Details

What counts as an episode. Episode 1 runs from time 0 to a subject's first row in data_events; episode k > 1 runs from the end of episode k - 1 to that subject's k-th row. A subject contributes no further episodes after a row with status %in% c(0, 2) (administrative censoring or a terminal event); any later rows for that id are ignored, with a message saying how many. status == 1 rows (recurrences) always start a new episode.

Feeding the result into survivalSub(). Fit the gap-time recurrence hazard and the recurrence-vs-terminal-event type model exactly as survivalSub() already fits a marginal hazard and a competing-risks type model, using episode_data in place of one-row-per-subject data, Surv(gap, event_any) ~ covariates in place of form_marginal_surv, and event_type ~ gap + covariates in place of form_conditional_cr (event_type is 0 for a recurrence, 1 for a terminal event – so predictRisk()'s risk_prob_1/risk_prob_2 come out as the recurrence/terminal risk respectively). Administratively-censored episodes get event_any = 0 and event_type = NA, exactly like status3 = 0/status4 = NA for a censored subject in pbc3. The episodes of one subject are then treated as independent: the coefficients are still consistent for the gap-time model, but the standard errors that summary() reports ignore the correlation between a subject's episodes and are too small.

Feeding the result into longitudinalSub()/predictRisk(). gap plays the same dual role years plays for pbc3: it is both the Surv() time in episode_data and the backward covariate swept over candidate values inside predictRisk(), so it must appear in long_sub_fixed (e.g. biomarker ~ time_in_episode + gap + gap * time_in_episode + covariates), and the training data passed to longitudinalSub() must be filtered to event_any == 1 rows of long_data – only completed episodes have an observed gap – exactly as the package's own examples filter pbc3 to status3 == 1 before fitting longitudinalSub(). time_in_episode (elapsed time since the current episode began) plays the role year plays for pbc3. To predict from "now" for a subject currently at risk in an open episode, add a trailing status = 0 row to data_events at the current data-cutoff time, and call predictRisk() with prediction_time set to that subject's elapsed time_in_episode at the cutoff.

Random effects: group by episode, not by patient. Fit the biomarker model with the random effects grouped by episode_id (random = ~ time_in_episode | episode_id), so that each episode is its own "subject", as it already is in the survival sub-model. A patient's biomarker level generally differs from one episode to the next (the underlying trajectory keeps moving), so a single random effect per patient is the wrong unit; in a simulation in which the biomarker's current level drives the risk, grouping by patient gave a clearly worse AUC than grouping by episode. predictRisk() and predictRecurrentCount() then take one episode_id per prediction, so give each prediction its own id.

The open episode's gap is NA. For an episode that has not ended (event_any == 0) – typically the one a subject is currently at risk in – the gap column of long_data is NA: its final length is exactly what is being predicted. predictRisk() reads a missing survival-time variable as "event time not yet known, still at risk", so that episode's rows can be passed straight to it, with no placeholder to set or override (episode_data keeps the real elapsed time of such an episode, which is what the Cox fit needs as a censoring time). Training rows are unaffected, since longitudinalSub() is fit on event_any == 1 rows only. Note that predictRisk() also expects the outcome columns it was fit with (the time and event-type variables) to exist in the prediction data; long_data already carries event_type (NA for an open episode).

Episodes that start at discharge (restart_variable, lookback). By default an episode starts at the previous event (time 0 for the first). For hospitalization data that is not the at-risk clock: after a readmission the patient is in hospital, not at risk, until discharge. Give data_events a numeric column – passed as restart_variable – holding, for each recurrence row, the time the process restarts (the discharge ending that stay); the next episode then starts there and its gap is measured from it. Time 0 is the first episode's start (e.g. the index discharge). Biomarkers measured during the stay, or before the index discharge, precede the episode they predict: lookback (default 0, none) keeps measurements up to that long before an episode's start – never reaching back past the previous event, so a stay's own labs are not mixed into the earlier at-risk period – and gives them negative time_in_episode. Use Inf to keep the whole stay (and, for the first episode, everything before time 0). Negative times are fine for longitudinalSub() and predictRisk().

Death, or the end of follow-up, during a hospital stay. With restart_variable, a terminal event or censoring row whose time is at or before the restart time of the readmission before it happened while the patient was in hospital, not at risk. That readmission then ends the subject's process: no further episode is opened, the row is dropped with a message, and so a death in hospital is not counted as an out-of-hospital terminal event (predictRecurrentCount()'s p_death is the probability of dying after discharge). Record such a stay's restart time as the time of death or of the end of follow-up, or later, when the discharge never happened. A data cutoff during a stay gives no open episode to predict for.

Covariates that change over time. Each episode's covariates come from the row of data_events that ends it, as in counting-process data, where each interval carries the covariate values in force during it. A covariate that changes over time must therefore be recorded on each row as its value at the start of that row's episode (age at the discharge that started it, the number of earlier admissions, the length of the previous stay), and the open episode's row in the same way. A value measured at the event itself – age at readmission, say – depends on how long the episode lasted, which is what the survival sub-model explains, and so biases it; a value measured at the time of the prediction is not what the model was fit with. Biomarkers that change within an episode belong in data_long. Covariates built from earlier episodes can also be added to episode_data afterwards, e.g. the length of the previous gap:

ed <- episodes$episode_data
ed$previous_gap <- ave(ed$gap, ed$id, FUN = function(g) c(0, g[-length(g)]))

Examples

## A minimal example: reshaping alone (no model fitting).
## Subject 1: two recurrences, then a terminal event; subject 2: censored.
data_events <- data.frame(
  id     = c(1, 1, 1, 2),
  time   = c(1.2, 2.5, 4.0, 3.1),
  status = c(1,   1,   2,   0),
  age    = c(58,  58,  58,  61)
)
episodes <- buildRecurrentEpisodes(data_events)
episodes$episode_data
#>   id episode episode_id gap event_any event_type age
#> 1  1       1        1:1 1.2         1          0  58
#> 2  1       2        1:2 1.3         1          0  58
#> 3  1       3        1:3 1.5         1          1  58
#> 4  2       1        2:1 3.1         0         NA  61

## Hospitalizations: each episode starts at DISCHARGE, not at the readmission.
## `time` = readmission (or death/censoring) day; `discharge` = day the stay
## it started ends. Labs drawn in the stay (and before the index discharge at
## day 0) are kept with negative time_in_episode via lookback = Inf.
events <- data.frame(id = 1, time = c(20, 60, 90), status = c(1, 1, 0),
                     discharge = c(26, 66, NA))
labs <- data.frame(id = 1, day = c(-3, 0, 5, 21, 26, 40, 61, 66, 80))
hf <- buildRecurrentEpisodes(events, labs, time_variable_long = "day",
                             restart_variable = "discharge", lookback = Inf)
hf$episode_data   # gaps measured from each discharge: 20, 34, 24
#>   id episode episode_id gap event_any event_type
#> 1  1       1        1:1  20         1          0
#> 2  1       2        1:2  34         1          0
#> 3  1       3        1:3  24         0         NA
hf$long_data[, c("day", "episode", "time_in_episode", "gap")]
#>   day episode time_in_episode gap
#> 1  -3       1              -3  20
#> 2   0       1               0  20
#> 3   5       1               5  20
#> 4  21       2              -5  34
#> 5  26       2               0  34
#> 6  40       2              14  34
#> 7  61       3              -5  NA
#> 8  66       3               0  NA
#> 9  80       3              14  NA

# \donttest{
## A full pipeline on simulated recurrent-event + longitudinal data:
## build episodes -> survivalSub() -> longitudinalSub() -> predictRisk() and
## predictRecurrentCount().
set.seed(1)
n <- 60
data_events <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(id) {
  k <- sample(1:3, 1)
  gaps <- rexp(k, rate = 1)
  data.frame(
    id = id, time = cumsum(gaps),
    status = c(rep(1, k - 1), sample(c(0, 2), 1, prob = c(0.6, 0.4))),
    age = round(50 + stats::rnorm(1, sd = 8)), sex = id %% 2
  )
}))

## subject 9999 is still at risk right now, 0.7 time units into their
## 2nd episode (1 prior recurrence, no resolution yet) -- this is who
## we will predict for below.
data_events <- rbind(data_events, data.frame(
  id = 9999, time = c(0.8, 1.6), status = c(1, 0), age = 55, sex = 1
))

data_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(seq_len(n), 9999), function(id) {
  maxt <- max(data_events$time[data_events$id == id]) + 0.2
  tt <- seq(0, maxt, by = 0.25)
  data.frame(id = id, year = tt, biomarker = rnorm(length(tt)))
}))

built <- buildRecurrentEpisodes(data_events, data_long, time_variable_long = "year")
#> buildRecurrentEpisodes(): dropped 50 row(s) of `data_long` whose year fell outside every modeled episode (before time 0 or the `lookback` window, inside a hospital stay not covered by `lookback`, or after the subject's recurrent-event process had already ended).

## gap-time recurrence hazard + recurrence-vs-terminal-event type model
survival_fit_recur <- survivalSub(
  built$episode_data,
  Surv(gap, event_any) ~ age + sex + episode,
  event_type ~ gap + age + sex + episode
)

## longitudinal sub-model, trained on completed episodes only, with the
## random effects grouped by episode (see Details)
long_fit_recur <- longitudinalSub(
  built$long_data[built$long_data$event_any == 1, ],
  biomarker ~ time_in_episode + age + sex + gap + gap * time_in_episode,
  ~ time_in_episode | episode_id
)

## subject 9999's open episode: its gap is NA, which predictRisk() reads as
## "still at risk" -- nothing to override
open <- built$long_data[built$long_data$id == 9999 & built$long_data$event_any == 0, ]
landmark <- max(open$time_in_episode)

## the risk that their *next* event, within 1 time unit, is a recurrence /
## a terminal event
risk <- predictRisk(
  open, long_fit_recur, survival_fit_recur,
  prediction_time = landmark, horizon = 1, time_variable = "time_in_episode",
  survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list(),
  bandcount1 = 10, bandcount2 = 10
)
risk$risk_prob_1 # P(next event within horizon is a recurrence)
#>    9999:2 
#> 0.2978591 
risk$risk_prob_2 # P(next event within horizon is the terminal event)
#>    9999:2 
#> 0.2763965 

## the number of recurrences over the next 3 time units
predictRecurrentCount(
  open, long_fit_recur, survival_fit_recur,
  prediction_time = landmark, horizon = 3, time_variable = "time_in_episode",
  n_sim = 100, seed = 1
)
#> Predicted recurrences in (0.7, 3.7], 1 patient(s), 100 simulated paths each
#> mean expected count 0.470; P(>=1) 0.380; P(>=2) 0.080; P(death) 0.890
#> 
#>  episode_id mean_count p_count_0 p_count_1 p_count_2 p_count_3plus p_ge1 p_ge2
#>      9999:2       0.47      0.62       0.3      0.07          0.01  0.38  0.08
#>  p_death
#>     0.89
# }
